`data/decisions/<id>.md`. Never edited by hand: it is a projection of those files and
adds no fact of its own. Regenerated at the end of every run. Nothing ever gates a
commit on whether it is current — if it is stale, run the command.*

This is the record of what was decided and why, including every small call made without
you. Standing decisions are grouped by the system they touch, in id order inside each
group. Superseded and withdrawn ones are listed at the end with the decision that
replaced each, so any id ever issued can still be found by searching this file for it.

# 00-CAR


## Fluids and service

*2 live — D-365 D-366*

**D-365 — The 3N71B gets ATF Type F, as the factory specifies; the Dexron VI bought is not for this box.** Camden's call, 2026-09-21, answering `CAR.01`: **"a"**. Closes `CAR.01`.

**The ruling.** Mazda specifies ATF Type F (Ford M2C33-F) for the 1982 3N71B automatic (`specs` SP-093, sources S-002 p.0-24 and S-003). Type F has no friction modifier. Dexron-family fluids soften this box's shifts and can make its bands slip, and there is no record of a rebuild with modern friction material that would allow them. So Type F goes in. The Valvoline Dexron VI / Mercon LV already bought (PH045, not fitted) is not used in this transmission: keep it for something else or return it.

**Why this is a decision in `00-CAR`.** It's a car-level service call, not part of any project, and `00-CAR` had no decisions table. One was added in this run so car-level rulings have a home. `00-CAR`'s fact tables still never cite a decision (§6.6, enforced by `check`): they state what the car takes, and this body says why.

**In the data.** `intervals` atf: spec is ATF Type F, and the "owner rules which" note is gone. `parts_history` PH045 marked "NOT for this transmission"; PH053 added, Type F to buy, 6.2 L for a full refill (SP-094). `specs` SP-147 folded into SP-094 (they were duplicates; SP-147 was kept only while this block cited it). New `00-CAR` table `decisions` (with `_tables` and `_schema` rows).
*2026-09-21 · closes CAR.01*

**D-366 — The oil metering pump is disconnected; the engine runs on premix in the fuel.** Camden's call, 2026-09-21, answering `CAR.02`: **"b"**. Closes `CAR.02`.

**The fact.** Option (b) of the block: "It's disconnected and the car runs on premix (2-stroke oil in the fuel)". On the 12A the oil metering pump fed engine oil into the factory carburettor to lubricate the apex seals (SP-024). The carburettor went with the Weber conversion (M-001), and the pump is disconnected. The apex seals now get their oil only from two-stroke oil mixed into the fuel.

**What it means.** Premix goes in at **every** fill-up, without exception. A tank without it runs the seals dry. That is now a service interval, not a habit.

**Still unknown.** The **ratio** isn't recorded anywhere. It's marked `confirm` in `intervals` premix and `mods` M-013. Camden knows it; it goes into those two rows the next time he says what he mixes. Also unknown is when the pump was disconnected (with the Weber, or after).

**In the data.** `as_fitted` Engine; `mods` M-013 (new); `intervals` premix (new, every fill); `specs` SP-024's note (the factory design, and what this car does instead).
*2026-09-21 · closes CAR.02*

# 00-electrical


## Architecture and scope

*15 live — D-001 D-002 D-004 D-007 D-081 D-119 D-131 D-194 D-202 D-209 D-211 D-213 D-228 D-259 D-374*

**D-001 — ECUMaster PMU-24 DL over a conventional relay/fuse box.** Accepted about $2,500 of premium for per-channel current logging, soft fuses set from measured draw, and logic without physical relays.

**D-002 — Ionic S9 heated lithium battery, rear-mounted.** Sold as "Ionic Lithium 12V S9 — Car Post Starter Heater Battery"; some listings say *S9H*. Same product. This project says "S9". The heater is why this model is right for a cold, high-altitude car: lithium must not be charged below freezing, and the heater warms the cells so it can (D-060).

**D-004 — All 39 PMU cavities are terminated at build time; reserved channels get real wire to the right housing and are capped there.** The 39-way connector is assembled once and never reopened.

**D-007 — Baseline pinned for the current 12A / Weber configuration; O13 and O14 (25 A) reserved for an engine swap's ECU and cooling fan, wired to the engine leg and capped.** The engine leg carries the reservation; its design lives in `../engine-swap/`.

**D-081 — The car drives fully on the PMU with plain switches, the factory harness comes out, and the build completes — then any module joins.** Modules add capability to a finished car; they are never a dependency for it starting, running or being legal. This is the whole reason the luxury package is a separate project.

**D-119 / D-124 — The car migrates and drives on stock incandescent bulbs.** Every lamp channel has 40–74 % headroom on filament bulbs, so nothing in the pin plan assumes LED. The custom tail lights, the headlamp change and the LED conversion are luxury-package scope; D-122 (soft fuses re-set after any bulb change) travels with them.

**D-131 — The windows are manual.** This car has no power-window motors, switches or wiring; the factory diagram's I-06/I-07/I-09/I-11 describe an option it does not have. Power windows are a luxury-package item. Nothing is deleted for it — every window conductor is run and capped (D-004), K5–K8 sockets and F8/F9 positions are provided at the sill, and adding motors later is plug in, populate, enable.

**D-194 — Configure in the car; there is no bench phase.** The PMU is mounted, powered from the new backbone through a 5 A fuse (D-145), and configured over CAN1 with every output disabled before any circuit migrates. Four bench-era rules survive as hard requirements: the 5 A first-power-up fuse; 120 Ω at both CAN1 ends or the client never connects; three practice crimps pull-tested before any real crimp; one circuit at a time, the car drives home every day.

**D-202 — One teardown: everything is bought now; measurements confirm before cutting, not before buying.** The interior comes apart once. Wire is bought with a 1.5× margin because the routes are unmeasured at order time; the dash envelope, the routes and the pop-up ohm check gate *cutting*, never purchasing. The drive-home rule survives throughout.

**D-209 — The column combination switch stays; every other switch in the car is replaced.** They are all broken or near it, and the dash opens once. Stays: E-01 LIGHT + DIMMER, F-02 TURN + HAZARD, D-03 wiper stalk — all laddered. The horn stays on the steering pad. Bought new: wink switches ×2, brake pedal switch, door-pin plungers, the ignition switch (electrical portion), the blower motor, resistor and speed switch.

**D-211 — The A/C system comes out; no cooling until the swap engine.** Compressor, bracket, belt, condenser, receiver/drier and lines are removed (a shop recovers the refrigerant first — venting it is illegal). The blower, heater core, HVAC case, ducts and blend doors stay, so heat, defrost and ventilation are unaffected. Electrically all subtractions: F4 and K10 deleted, the factory interlock chain leaves with the hardware, no cavity moves. **Nothing is capped for it in the engine bay** — the engine leg carries only what the engine on the mounts needs and is rebuilt from scratch at a swap. Its return is `../engine-swap/`.

**D-213 — One wiring project.** `electrical-build/` owns the harness — design, shopping, install — as a three-step guide with `DECISIONS.md` and `QUESTIONS.md` at its root. `luxury-package/` owns every future feature (heated/cooled seats, the digital cluster ICU, the climate module DCU, the control panel, defog trigger, mirrors, windows, sound deadening, LED lighting); `engine-swap/` owns everything that changes with the engine (ECU, CAN drop, in-tank pump, A/C's return, transmission, axle). The old `electrical-pmu/` tree is dissolved: its history and process files are archived under `../../99-ARCHIVE/Electrical/2026-09-02_electrical-pmu/` and stay linkable; its firmware and module designs moved to the luxury package. Answers Q-072.
*2026-09-02*

**D-228 — The A/C compressor runs on its own belt; the D-211 strip is purely subtractive.** Confirmed at the crank pulley, 2026-09-03. Nothing else is driven off that belt, so removing the compressor and bracket needs no shorter belt and does not touch the alternator or water-pump drive. Answers V-097.
*2026-09-03 · closes V-097*

**D-259 — The ICU is a device of this build: designed, built, bench-commissioned against the old cluster and installed with the harness, so the car's instruments run through it from the first drive; the luxury package supplies only the display that ribbons onto it later. D-081 is amended to "the car drives fully on the PMU *and the ICU*".** Camden's call, 2026-09-07, answering `Q-122` — "the ICU is done and seamless before luxury starts; only the display comes with luxury, and the screen wiring is already done." D-081's principle — modules add capability to a finished car and are never a dependency for it starting, running or being legal — holds word for word: the ICU is not a control source (D-251), the fuel-pump gate is the PMU's own A7 on a node the PMU excites (D-249, D-260), and a dead ICU costs the driver his gauges — exactly what a dead factory cluster would have cost, accepted. What changes is *who builds it and when*: the carrier `H-001`, its channels, its parts (`P103`–`P114`), its bench commissioning (install §1.20–1.24) and the questions in front of its layout (`Q-123`, `V-073`, `V-082`, `V-057`, `Q-304`, `Q-308`, `Q-309`) are this project's; the luxury package keeps the display chain (`T-051`, `V-084`, `V-085`), the pages, the DCU and everything comfort (luxury D-313 is the hand-over). The firmware stays one source in the luxury tree (`01-DESIGN/firmware/icu/`, R6) — its sensing, CAN and gauge-drive half is now this project's specification (`icu_channels.csv`), its rendering half theirs. The display header, the PSRAM, the IMU and the page-button header go on the board now, so it never comes out for the display.
*2026-09-07*

**D-374 — The ICU and the DCU are both this build's, whole: boards, channels, enclosures, connectors, firmware, the panel's electronics and the CAN bus map. The DCU goes into the car with the harness. The luxury package keeps only the loads the DCU drives and the plastics.** Camden's call, 2026-09-22, in chat: *"there seems to be some confusion about the dcu, the ice is full go now, just the fancy parts it controls are in luxry. make sure all of the icu is part of electrical, and icu and dcu ensure both are in the kad information and both wired and dialed inside electrical"*.

**How his words are read.** "The ice is full go now" is read as *the DCU is full go now*: the sentence is about the DCU, and the rest of it ("just the fancy parts it controls are in luxury") only makes sense of the DCU. The ICU was already this build's (D-259), and his next sentence covers it separately. "Dialed" is read as *detailed*, meaning every channel of the DCU is specified here the way `icu_channels` specifies the ICU's. "The kad information" is `cad/`. Nothing in this reading buys, cuts or rewires anything. It moves rows between two projects of the same car, and every consequence below can be undone by editing rows.

**Why the confusion was real.** The luxury package owned the DCU (luxury D-075, and D-313 "keeps … the DCU"), but the rulings since have routed basic functions through it. The window commands (D-363), the hatch and fuel-door selects (D-370), the panel's keys, among them defog (luxury D-355), and the wake request (D-350) all have no path except the DCU. A car whose harness is finished but whose DCU belongs to a later project can't open its hatch from the panel. The DCU is part of the electrical system. Only the loads it drives are luxury.

**The boundary.**
- **This build**: both modules, whole. Carriers H-001 and H-002, their channels (`icu_channels`, and the new `dcu_channels`), enclosures, DT13 receptacles, the DCU's comfort receptacle, their firmware (the pages included), the control panel's electronics (keys, encoders, thumbstick, ribbon: the panel is the DCU's input device), the bench kit, the bring-up log, and the one CAN map. The map moves because every node on CAN2 is now this build's: PMU, ICU, DCU and wideband.
- **The luxury package**: every load the DCU drives (blower and final stage, HVAC servos, seat heat and cool, the mirror heads and heat pads, window motors and regulators, the release relays K3/K4 and the solenoids' test), the O15 comfort block and the harness from it to the DCU's comfort receptacle (luxury LP49), radar, lighting, and every visible plastic: the display bezel and the panel's faceplate and knobs.

**Supersedes** luxury D-313 and D-314, which split the ICU and kept its pages, the display chain's firmware, the CAN map and the DCU in the luxury package. What they moved stays moved. The display, its eval board, its glass and the carrier are this build's (D-268). The bezel stays the luxury package's (luxury FT34, H-006). The Q-302 ruling stands (the backlight is the F16 ignition aux on `DP-ICU-A 6`, D-258). D-361's "the DCU (luxury `H-002`)" and D-362's "the mating harness half is this project's" are narrowed: `H-002` is this build's, and the harness half from the O15 block stays the luxury package's.

**The DCU goes in with the harness.** Its tails (`DP-DCU`, `DP-DCU-B`) were dust-capped at the centre stack "until S2". Now it plugs in at install step E26, beside the ICU. `DP-DCU 1–6` are LIVE from install, as `DP-ICU-A` is: F22 was already LIVE, sized for the DCU (D-355). `DP-DCU-B` stays CAPPED, since its far ends wait capped for loads the luxury package fits later. The DCU on the bench and in the car drives lamps and capped lines until then. This makes install wait on the DCU (E26 gates on F6). That is what "full go" costs, and it's the same position the ICU is in.

**In the data.**
- **Moved from luxury, numbers kept** (`work`): F-001, F-005–F-017, B5, B7, B8, H-002, H-007, X-007, Z-003, V-083, V-100–V-102, T-048, T-049 into stage F (retitled "The ICU and the DCU"); V-065, Q-028 into stage V. Gates re-qualified: H-002 now waits on `01-luxury:W-332`, F-015 on `W-330`, F4 on `F-012`. Added **F5** (order and build H-002, yours) and **F6** (bench-commission the DCU, yours). **E26** now plugs in the DCU too and waits on F6. Luxury keeps its history rows (A1–A12, X-006, H-003, the dropped ones), its loads' rows and the bezel.
- **Parts**: luxury LP01, LP02, LP04 → P142, P143, P151 (bench). LP06–LP09, LP11, LP14, LP45–LP47, LP22 → P144–P150, P152–P154 (the DCU). LP20's electronics, LP35, LP50 → P155–P157 (the panel). LP03 folded into P070, which it always was. LP20 stays luxury as the faceplate and knobs, unpriced until H-007. LP49 stays luxury, mating P153.
- **Tables moved whole**: luxury `sensors` became `dcu_channels` here, in `icu_channels`'s shape (SN11–SN23, ids kept), plus SN24–SN27 for the power, ground, bus and servo/comfort supply that the old table left out (from D-355, D-273, D-346 and the V-083 note; SN27's pinout is `confirm` until V-101). `modules`, `can_messages`, `can_fields` and `bringup_log` moved unchanged except for the module rows' ownership text. `params` merged into this build's, which gained `unit` and `source` columns.
- **Luxury**: `features` FT07–FT11, FT15 and FT33 marked moved. FT14 is now the faceplate. `provisions` PV26–PV30, PV32, PV33, PV114–PV122 and PV127 deleted: they described the DCU's own drop as something the luxury package counted on, and it is now this build's own device. The provisions at the loads' end (mirror lines, window commands, mirror-heat feed) stay. `stages` S0 is delivered by this build, and S2 is the blower, servos and faceplate. `_project` goals rewritten on both sides.
- **This build**: `devices` DV54 (the DCU) added. DV53's stale "window switch pack lives here" is corrected (D-362 moved those lines to `DP-DCU-B`). The `cavities`, `node_conductors`, `housings`, `P140` and `E17` notes that said "until S2" now say E26.
- **Outside the record**: `firmware/` moved from `01-luxury/` to here with its history (`git mv`), and its README's paths were updated. `cad/README.md` and `PCB-AND-3D-GUIDE.md` Part B now point at this build's rows. `cad/dcu-carrier/` was started with `README.md` and `TARGET.md` (the checklist from `dcu_channels`). The schematic starts when V-083, V-101, H-007 and luxury W-332 are in.

## Build sequence

*16 live — D-023 D-025 D-127 D-143 D-146 D-176 D-177 D-322 D-323 D-344 D-353 D-367 D-371 D-372 D-386 D-387*

**D-023 / D-024 — Parallel-system migration, least to most consequential, ending with ignition and start.** The factory harness stays intact and powered until each circuit's own cutover; never both systems on one load; the car drives home at the end of every session.

**D-025 / D-174 — Soft fuses are set from current measured live in the client during migration, never from an estimate; the PMU's telemetry on the new harness is the measurement, and its gap against healthy-expected draw is also the list of tired parts to replace afterwards.**

**D-127 / D-137 / D-103 — Housekeeping that stands: verify the two spare housings' terminal counts on arrival; mark cavity 1 on the housing with the paint pen before the first terminal goes in (D-139); measure the pop-up motors and check the transit contacts in one sitting.**

**D-143 / D-145 — The deliberate soft-fuse trip is a required step, done in the car on the first migrated circuit (the interior lamp): set the limit to 2 A, short the output, watch it trip and retry.** It is the single behaviour that distinguishes this device from a fuse box and it must be met on purpose, not at speed.

**D-146 — Powered verification of the dash node is replaced by continuity testing, which needs no power and catches a wrong cavity, a missed crimp, a swapped pair and a short to the panel.** Powered checks happen in the car with every output disabled.

**D-176 — Part replacement (a slow wiper motor, a weak pump) is a separate job after the PMU is in, identified from telemetry — not clutter inside the wiring project.**

**D-177 / D-199 — The pop-up motor pinout comes from factory sheet E (E-03 / E-04: YG top · WR left · RY right · R bottom; YG is the cam-driven transit contact the ladders read; WR is the constant feed and is capped). Which of R / RY carries the run winding through the cam — bridged or single — is decided by the ohm check at the motor (install M-3), the one measurement the pin plan waits on.**

**D-322 — Limp-home is the config file and a USB-to-CAN cable carried in the car, plus a one-page written emergency procedure.** Camden's call, 2026-09-11, answering `00.09`: "follow recommendation (i cant afford a spare pmu so definitely give my a way to fix small pmu issues on the go or enable limp mode under worse cases)."

No PDM vendor documents a bypass, backup module or manual override; the corpus treats total module failure as accepted risk and the professional mitigation is a spare configured unit. That is a **racing** answer. This is a street-registered car where brake lamps, ignition and fuel pump are all software-defined on one module that is not automotive-qualified and lives in a 44-year-old dash — and option (c), a spare PMU, is explicitly out on cost.

So options **(a) + (b)** together, which cost a cable and an afternoon: the configuration file and a USB-to-CAN cable **live in the car**, so a soft fault — a mis-set soft fuse, a tripped channel, a bad expression — is fixed at the roadside; and a **one-page written emergency procedure** covers the hard case, feeding fuel pump, ignition and brake lamps directly from the busbar to get the car home. The design had none of the three. Recovery from a *single* dead output is separate and already possible (D-282).

**In the data.** The cable becomes a `parts` row. The procedure is agent work (`W-322`) and lands in the install record when the install steps exist; it is written before first power-up, not after.
*2026-09-11 · closes 00.09*

**D-323 — Nothing is bought until the design is complete and Camden understands it; no cart is paid early.** Camden's call, 2026-09-11, answering `00.10`: "Rule everything first i do not want to buy anything until the plan is detail for detail flawless and i undersatand like its already physcaly in the car and working perfectly."

This **overrides the packet's own recommendation**, which was to pay Waytek, WireBarn and DeutschConnector immediately and hold only the Amazon cart. The recommendation optimised for lead time; he is optimising for understanding, and understanding is the thing that cannot be bought twice.

**What it means in practice.** `A1` (pay the four carts) is blocked on the design freeze, not on the four packets that were in front of it. No store is paid while any block that changes a line is open, and the long-lead Deutsch order waits with the rest. The comprehension bar is his, not the checker's: the plan reads as though the car is already built and working, or it is not done.

**Why it costs less than it looks.** D-202's one-teardown logic is untouched — everything is still bought in one pass, the pass simply moves later. The four parts that were about to be bought twice (P049's switch under `00.12`, P052's fuse under D-321, the battery-data source under `00.11`) are exactly the ones this prevents. Nothing in the design depends on parts arriving before the freeze.

**In the data.** `work` `A1` → blocked, gate `design freeze`. The phase gate into SOURCING now carries this decision by name, so no future run can read an empty §1 as permission to pay.
*2026-09-11 · closes 00.10*

**D-344 — The limp-home procedure is a table inside the record, not a document; the glovebox kit is three parts; and writing it out found one thing the ruling could not have known.** Agent, 2026-09-12, carrying out `W-322` under D-322.

D-322 ruled that the config file and a USB-to-CAN cable live in the car, plus "a one-page written emergency procedure" feeding fuel pump, ignition and brake lamps directly from the busbar. It also said the procedure "lands in the install record when the install steps exist". The install steps do not exist as rows in v3, and a page written outside the record would be the fifth thing to keep in step with it, so the procedure is a **table**: `recovery`, ten rows, `RC01`–`RC10`, ordered, with a `situation` of *always*, *soft fault* or *dead module*. It prints from the record, so the copy in the glovebox can never quietly diverge from the design.

**What it says, in short.** RC01 is the disconnect, first, before anything, and it says why: a high-side MOSFET fails **short**, so an output can be live with the key out (D-336). RC02 separates a soft fault from a dead module in one look. RC03–RC05 are the roadside fix: laptop on `DP-DIAG`, read `pmu.status` and the per-output status, force the channel or raise that one soft fuse, drive home, and put it back. RC06–RC09 are the dead-module branch: confirm the module and not its supply, then three temporary busbar feeds — fuel pump on the O5 conductor at 10 A, ignition on O12 at **20 A** because it also carries F15's excitation and F16, brake lamps on O7 at 10 A — landed on the conductors at the node, never on the module's pins, with the module's own output disconnected so a half-dead PMU cannot back-feed. RC08 says plainly that the disconnect is now the key. RC10 says a limp-home wire left in place is the next fault.

**The thing D-322 could not have known.** There is **nothing to switch the brake lamps with.** The brake pedal switch F-11 is a ladder contact — 4.7 kΩ to ground into A3 — and the spare P084 plunger beside it is a wake contact at the same signal level. Neither carries lamp current and neither ever will; that is what a ladder is. So a direct feed lights both brake lamps and leaves them lit: rear presence, no brake indication. RC09 says so in those words rather than pretending otherwise, and whether the kit gains a lamp-rated second pedal plunger — fitted at install while the pedal box is open, unwired until needed — is **`00.16`**.

**In the data.** New table `recovery`, RC01–RC10. `parts` P138 the USB-to-CAN cable and P139 the three-holder kit, both glovebox items that are never fitted to the car.
*2026-09-12*

**D-353 — The dead-module limp keeps two feeds, not three. The brake-lamp feed is dropped rather than run constant, and a pair of beacons goes in the bag instead.** Camden's call, 2026-09-13, answering `00.16`: option (a), modified. Closes `00.16`.

In his words: *"(a), modified — accept the dead-module limp, and **drop the brake-lamp feed** rather than run it constant. No plunger, no toggle, no change at the pedal."*

**Why not the recommendation.** `00.16` recommended (c), a second lamp-rated plunger on the brake pedal, fitted while the pedal box is open and left unwired until needed. He rejected it as *"the right answer to the wrong question: it spends a part, a conductor stub and a line of install section 3 to improve a failure that is the least likely of the three PMU failure modes, behind config faults (already covered by RC03–RC05) and harness faults (RC06 already separates these)."* And he rejected running the feed constant on the grounds the block itself raised but did not follow to its conclusion: *"A constantly-lit brake lamp is not rear presence, it is false brake indication, and the drive it exists for is daylight, dry and short — where it buys close to nothing."*

**The reasoning that makes this consistent rather than a retreat.** D-322 found that no PDM vendor documents a bypass and that the industry treats total module failure as accepted risk; a spare configured unit is the professional mitigation and is out on cost. *"This car accepts it too, on the same terms as the fuel pump, the alternator and the coil. The limp kit stays only because it is a ziploc bag that costs ~$18 and no install time — cheap enough to carry, not important enough to build the car around."*

**And it moves the answer to where the hazard actually is.** *"The real hazard is not the drive home, it is being stopped and dark, and that is answered by visibility in the kit rather than by a switch on the pedal."* Magnetic LED beacons or a reflective triangle, $15–25, carried and never fitted.

**In the data.** `recovery` RC07 — two feeds: fuel pump on the `O5` conductor at 10 A, landing on K13 terminal 87 (D-352), and ignition on the `O12` conductor at 20 A, which carries F15's excitation and F16 as well as the coils. The brake feed and its 10 A holder are gone; the landing rule is unchanged. `recovery` RC09 — brake lamps, tail and park join the list of what you do not have, the "ON CONSTANTLY" paragraph and the pointer to this block are deleted, and the beacons instruction goes in. `recovery` RC10 — the bag's contents. `parts` P139 — two holders, not three, plus the beacons. **Install section 3: no change**, and D-278 stands exactly as written — one spare P084 plunger as the wake contact, and any 2-terminal P085 as the stop-lamp switch.

**One thing he added that is worth more than the part the block was arguing about.** *"Commissioning — add a one-time check: pull the PMU's feed in daylight, run RC07, confirm the car starts, runs and drives on the two temporary feeds, then restore. Proving the procedure once is worth more than any part this block considered."* That is **`CK11`**, and it is timed: if it takes more than about twenty minutes at a warm bench it will not happen at the roadside in the rain.

Nothing else moves. `loads` LD03, `logic` BRAKE, `inputs` A3 and `ladders` A3 are untouched — the brake lamps remain a PMU channel driven from the A3 ladder, which is correct whenever the module is alive, and that is every drive but one.

**D-367 — The limp-home fuel-pump feed lands on K13 terminal 30, so the key still switches the pump.** Camden's call, 2026-09-21, answering `00.20`: **"a"**. Closes `00.20`.

**The problem.** `recovery` RC07, the dead-module limp home, said to land the temporary fused fuel-pump feed "on K13 terminal 87, DOWNSTREAM of the series relay, so the key still gates the pump" (D-352). But 87 is K13's output, straight on to the pump (N70). Power landed there skips the relay's contact, so the key gated nothing, and RC08 said the pump was live whenever the disconnect was closed. That defeats K13, the ignition-switch back-stop D-352 added for exactly this case.

**The ruling.** The feed lands on **K13 terminal 30**, its input, where the O5 conductor (N69) normally arrives, with the PMU's O5 end lifted. K13's coil is fed from the ignition switch (N71), not the PMU, so it works with the module dead. The pump runs only with the key in RUN, as it does when the PMU is alive. Turning the key off starves the engine and it stops within seconds. Ignition (coils, F15, F16) is still live while the disconnect is closed, so the disconnect is opened whenever the car is left.

**In the data.** `recovery` RC07 (terminal 30, with "never on 87") and RC08 (the key still stops the engine; the disconnect makes it safe to leave). CK11, which proves the procedure once on the drive, now tests the corrected version.

## Legs, connectors and grounds

*47 live — D-017 D-029 D-032 D-034 D-045 D-065 D-069 D-092 D-115 D-159 D-171 D-217 D-218 D-232 D-250 D-252 D-254 D-255 D-258 D-260 D-261 D-262 D-263 D-264 D-265 D-266 D-267 D-268 D-269 D-270 D-271 D-272 D-273 D-274 D-281 D-283 D-317 D-329 D-339 D-350 D-360 D-377 D-378 D-379 D-380 D-382 D-385*

**D-017 / D-037 — Grounds never cross a leg connector; every zone has one star node straight to bare chassis (engine block, front stud, dash-node ground bus, rear stud, sill stud); pin 25 is the only PMU ground and carries every flyback return.** The five dash-post drops are the one exception: their grounds cross a connector because they are devices inches from the node with no zone of their own.

**D-029 — Four legs, cut by removal boundary, not connector convenience: L1 engine (the firewall grommet), L2 front (nose, bumper, pop-ups), L3 dash, L4 rear (tunnel to hatch, plus the sill).**

**D-032 / D-033 — Power and signal get separate housings on every leg (terminal size, noise, and service — diagnosing a switch must not break a 25 A circuit), coded `L<leg>-<class><index>`: P = 12 AWG power, M = 14–16 AWG medium, S = signal. Leg side is always the socket housing (`06-…S`), dash-node side always the pin housing (`04-…P`), so a leg cannot be plugged into the wrong half.**

**D-034 / D-052 / D-070 / D-219 — Every housing is genuine Deutsch: DTP (size 12) for `-P`, DT (size 16) for everything else, DP-DIAG and DP-KEY included.** No AMPSEAL, and no DTM: the two 4-way ports were carted as DT 4-way on 2026-09-02 so every contact in the car is size 12 or size 16 and there is no size-20 tooling. L3-S is 2 × DT06-12S + 1 × DT06-8S — cheaper and easier to source than one large housing, and a failure takes out part of the dash rather than all of it.
*2026-09-02*

**D-045 / D-046 / D-134 / D-139 — The 39-way connector is 3 rows × 13, numbered left → right, top → bottom viewed at the device, with pin 1 top-left at the end furthest from the purple lock. Each row is 2 large · 9 small · 2 large: the twelve 2.8 mm cavities are pins 1, 2, 12, 13, 14, 15, 25, 26, 27, 28, 38, 39.** Confirmed on the physical part against the ECUmaster manual. Consequence: every 15 A and 7 A output sits in a 1.5 mm cavity limited to 13–17 AWG, so 14 AWG on O6–O11 is the maximum, and pin 15 (+5 V) needs the 2.8 mm 16 AWG terminal despite its small current.

**D-065 / D-067 / D-068 / D-132 — The sill node: window relays K5–K8 and fuses F8/F9 belong at the sill (dry, accessible, short motor legs), the doors get their own connector pair there (D1/D2), and the node is built now — sockets fitted empty, fuse positions labelled — even though nothing on it is live.** Building it behind a trim panel on a finished car costs an afternoon; building it now costs a few dollars.

**D-069 — Pop-up relays stay at the dash node, not in the nose.** The nose is the wettest, hottest, most vibration-exposed part of the car.

**D-092 / D-093 — One DT06-08S per door: two 14 AWG window-motor legs, a spare, three mirror-motor conductors, mirror heat, and the door ground to the sill stud.** Independent wiring per side; the factory multiplexed mirror switch is dead and the mirrors will be new.

**D-115 / D-116 / D-117 / D-118 — DTP is manufactured in 2-way and 4-way only; size 16 seals 14–20 AWG and size 12 seals 10–14 AWG (14 AWG in a DT is at the top of the seal range — fine, no margin above); the C015 reduced-diameter seal exists if 16 AWG GXL seals loosely; secondary wedgelocks are separate parts and are in the kits.**

**D-159 — The future cluster display does not cross the harness.** DP-ICU carries power, ground, CAN2, the illumination reference and the sensor taps; a display needs a high-speed bus and belongs inches from its controller behind the same bezel.

**D-171 / D-172 — L1-S is two DT06-12S (L1-S1, L1-S2) and L3-S is three housings, allocated as the design's cavity tables show; every cavity carries a status word so a capped wire is never mistaken for a spare.**

**D-217 — L2 has one power housing, L2-P (DTP 4-way): headlight LOW, headlight HIGH, pop-up LH run, pop-up RH run. L2-P2 is deleted.** The second DTP shell existed for reversible pop-up motors; D-186 made them single-direction, so the front needs four size-12 conductors and one shell holds them. The 2026-09-02 cart carries three DTP-4 pairs (L1-P, L2-P, L4-P). Closes the D-208(d) finding.
*2026-09-02*

**D-218 — A spare cavity gets sealing plugs in both halves, not a capped wire. CAPPED is reserved for a named future feature.** A capped spare costs wire, two contacts, two labels and crimping time for a cavity nothing is planned for; a plug costs cents and the housing stays sealed. Named features (windows, mirrors, solenoids, the module drops, the swap reservations) keep their capped conductors so no later project touches the harness. 64 size-16 plugs carted. Supersedes D-022.
*supersedes D-022*

**D-232 — The gauge rule is set by the enable-at limit, not the channel's rating.** 2026-09-03, a clarification the automated check forced: `DESIGN.md` §13 said "12 AWG on 25 A, 14 AWG on 15 A", and four rows already broke it on purpose — the 16 AWG high-beam-indicator tap on O3 and the three 16 AWG capped module drops on O10. A wire has to survive what its protection lets through, and the protection is the software limit: 12 AWG above 15 A, 14 AWG above 13 A, 16 AWG at 13 A and below. A 16 AWG tap off a heavier feed is allowed only where the cavity notes it as a tap, and the check flags any other case. No wire changes.
*2026-09-03*

**D-250 — The engine leg carries a switched sensor supply and two signal spares for the ICU's Phase-2 sensors: `L1-S2 9` (+12 V, RED), `L1-S2 10` (oil temperature, GRY) and `L1-S2 11` (spare, GRY), capped 12 in past the grommet like the swap reserves.** Camden's call, 2026-09-07, answering `Q-111` with (b) — and (a) with it: the three original senders are replaced now with factory-spec resistive parts, fitted *before* the in-car calibration reads, and the tank sender's curve is re-measured after the swap, not before. A 3-wire transducer or a thermistor with a published curve wants a regulated supply, a signal and a ground where this design runs one wire; the cavities were free but the supply was not, and adding it later means the firewall grommet, the leg and the dash. No +5 V goes down the leg (D-215 stands): the supply is switched 12 V from a spare block-B fuse position, fitted only when a sensor arrives, regulated at the sender or the dash node, and the same position also feeds the road-speed sensor (`L4-S 4`, D-252). At the dash node the two signals land on `DP-ICU-B 7` and `9` (`N65`, `N67`); the supply is capped at the node (`N68`). Three cavities that were sealing plugs, six size-16 contacts from spares, about forty feet of 16 AWG inside the wire margin.
*2026-09-07 · closes Q-111*

**D-252 — The ICU drop is two housings, not one: `DP-ICU-A`, a DT-6 carrying power and bus, and `DP-ICU-B`, a DT-12 carrying only sensors.** Camden's call, 2026-09-07, answering `Q-117`. After the fuel tap (D-251) the single DT-12 had one cavity left, and the ICU's own `0x200` frame already expects oil temperature and road speed — neither had a conductor or a cavity. `DP-ICU-A` is cavity-for-cavity the DP-DCU pattern (1 +12 V switched off O10 · 3 ground · 4 CAN2 H · 5 CAN2 L) plus the illumination reference on 2 and a plug on 6, so every module in the car plugs into the same six-way and only the ICU has a second, sensor-only housing. `DP-ICU-B`: 1 water temp · 2 oil pressure · 3 fuel level · 4 tach · 5 charge sense · 6 brake warning — the six taps — then 7 oil temperature (`L1-S2 10`, D-250) · 8 road-speed signal (`L4-S 3`) · 9 Phase-2 spare (`L1-S2 11`) · 10–12 plugs. Road speed gets two 16 AWG conductors in L4 now — `L4-S 3` signal, `L4-S 4` sensor supply, capped in the tunnel at the transmission's speedo drive with a service loop — because no road-speed signal exists on this car (the speedometer is cable-driven) and L4 already runs the tunnel; if an inline sensor fits at the speedometer head behind the dash (checked at M-2) they stay capped forever and nothing is lost. A Hall or open-collector sensor is what they suit; a VR sensor would need a shielded pair that is not provided. *Old → new:* DP-ICU 1 → A 1 · 2 → A 3 · 3 → A 4 · 4 → A 5 · 5 → A 2 · 6 → B 1 · 7 → B 2 · 8 (plug) → B 3 fuel · 9 → B 4 · 10 (plug) → B 8 road speed · 11 → B 5 · 12 → B 6 — any older text citing a `DP-ICU n` reads through this table, and "the five drops" of D-017/D-037 are six housings. *Cart:* one DT06-6S / DT04-6P assembly-kit pair and a 6-way dust cap join the DeutschConnector line — a few dollars. *Supersedes* D-215's "DP-ICU is the 12-way sensor drop"; D-159 (the display never crosses the harness) is unchanged and is what makes the display a bezel-only event whenever the dash design is ready.
*2026-09-07 · closes Q-117*

**D-254 — `L4-P 4` is the O15 comfort feed to the sill: 12 AWG off the O15 splice at the dash node, capped at the sill node, the source of F14 (mirror heat).** Camden's call, 2026-09-07, answering `Q-118`. D-181 drew this feed; D-215 re-purposed the cavity for the amplifier constant and D-230, deleting the amp, plugged it as "a heavy cavity with no named future feature" — but mirror heat is a named future feature and F14 had been left with no source, a run under the sill trim waiting to happen. Restored: `N17` is a splice to `L3-P 2` and `L4-P 4`; the luxury package's DCU switches mirror heat at the dash, downstream of O15, through this conductor. About fifteen feet of 12 AWG and two size-12 contacts; `P029` drops to L1-P 4's plugs alone. *Supersedes* D-230's "L4-P 4 stays plugged" and D-215's "D-181's O15 → sill feed is not run".
*2026-09-07 · closes Q-118*

**D-255 — A second L4 signal housing, `L4-S2` (DT-8), carries the mirror-adjust commands from the dash post to the sill: 1 shared common · 2 LEFT X · 3 LEFT Y · 4 RIGHT X · 5 RIGHT Y · 6–8 plugs; capped at the post, spliced at the sill node onto `D1 4–6` and `D2 4–6`.** Camden's call, 2026-09-07, answering `Q-119`. The doors had their motor conductors (D-093, D-305) and nothing drove them: no dash → sill command existed, and after D-252 `L4` had no spare size-16 cavity, so a dash switch or the DCU could never have moved a mirror without a new run under the sill trim. Five conductors because the two mirrors' commons share one wire when a single switch or driver serves both. A mechanical mirror switch in the panel or the DCU's bridge outputs land on the post receptacle later — dash-node work, no leg touched. **D-258 — The factory cluster is a peripheral of the ICU, not of the harness: there is no cluster drop. Every conductor the cluster used to receive terminates at `DP-ICU-A` / `DP-ICU-B`; the ICU excites and reads the fuel and water-temp senders, reads the PMU-excited oil node, drives the cluster's three gauges as a programmable sender (a low-side PWM sink in place of the resistance each gauge used to see) and passes the tach, charge, brake and tell-tale lines straight through — all on a twelve-line CLU pigtail built from the cluster's own connector. `DP-ICU-A 6` is the F16 ignition aux (the cluster's feed now, the display's backlight later); `DP-ICU-B 10–12` are the turn-L, turn-R and high-beam tell-tale senses, tapped off O17, O18 and O3.** Camden's call, 2026-09-07, answering `Q-121`: yes to the ICU taking the cluster's role, with the constraint that the old cluster is intentionally temporary and must leave *without a trace* — no wire in the harness that only it used. A DT-12 drop for the cluster would have been exactly such a trace: twelve conductors and a receptacle on the post with nothing to plug in once the display arrived. Routing the same signals to the ICU instead costs nothing — `DP-ICU-B` already carried six taps on them — and buys three things: the ICU is the single exciter and reader of every sender from day one (no high-impedance observer front end, no calibration against a gauge regulator's pulsing, no hand-over of excitation later — luxury D-310 and Q-301 become moot); the needles can be linearised in software for the first time; and the day the display goes in, one pigtail unplugs. The cluster's own regulator still powers its coils and lamps, from the F16 aux through the ICU. *In the data:* `DP-CLU` and its twelve cavities are deleted (the DT-12 kit pair leaves the Deutsch count; `MG03` / `MG22` re-drawn); `N20`, `N22`, `N45`–`N53`, `N59`, `N64` re-point; `DV32` becomes "temporary, on the ICU's pigtail" and `DV45` is the ICU; `P074`'s shielded cable ends at `DP-ICU-B 4`; the ICU's channels are a new table, `data/icu_channels.csv`, rendered as `01-DESIGN/ICU-CARRIER.md`. Whether the gauges are bimetal or air-core decides the drive stage's PWM frequency, not its topology — `Q-123`, one look at M-6. *Supersedes* D-215's "DP-CLU feeds the factory cluster from day one" and D-252's `DP-ICU-B 10–12` (plugs → tell-tale senses) and `DP-ICU-A 6` (plug → F16 aux); D-252's old → new table still reads for cavities 1–9.
*2026-09-07*

**D-260 — The oil-pressure node is excited by the PMU, not the ICU: a 100 Ω 1 W pull-up from pin 15 (+5 V) to the node, on the dash node beside the two bias resistors. A7 keeps its 1 MΩ pull-down; the ICU reads the same node with no pull-up of its own.** 2026-09-07 — the one exception to D-258's "the ICU excites the senders", forced by D-251: the fuel-pump gate reads this node, and a gate whose excitation came from the ICU would depend on the ICU — reboot the module and the pump stops five seconds later. With the PMU exciting it, A7 reads a clean DC node whatever the ICU is doing; the ICU is the second reader and drives the old gauge from what it reads. An open sender wire reads full scale and a short reads zero, both outside any real sender value, so both are FAULT windows and fail open (D-249); the old gauge's pulsing regulator is gone from the node, so the reading is steadier than it was. **D-317 — Future circuits run both conductors down the leg and branch only what the fitted part needs; the wiper park sense is the first case.** Camden's call, 2026-09-11, answering `00.02`: "follow recommendations, prepare for both wires through the front leg, however when the wiper branches off solo only the one needed wire continues after the branch to the part, then if I use other wipers I just pull that tiny branch and pin the second wire (all casis/body/intitor shoud follow this patter for future circuts)."

**The rule, for every chassis, body and interior circuit.** The leg carries **both** conductors as far as the branch point. Past the branch, only the conductor the fitted part actually uses continues to the part. The spare stays unpinned at the branch. Changing to a part that needs the other conductor is then a short branch pulled and a second contact pinned — never a leg re-run. This refines D-274, which ended a future circuit in half a connector where it left its leg: D-274 still governs a circuit whose part does not exist yet, and D-317 governs a circuit whose part exists but whose *variant* may change.

**The wiper case.** Replacement two-speed motors sort into five families. The fitted Japanese OE motor brings the cam out as a **dry SPDT**, which is what the A3 ladder assumes and is correct. The commonest universal on the shelf is the **Bosch/SWF/Valeo DIN 72552** family, which self-parks: the cam's common is the **low-brush node**, `53a` wants a permanent +12 and `53e` is the brake throw — reading either would put battery volts and brush spikes onto A3.

**In the data.** `L2-S 4` is promoted from sealing plug to a `WIPER_PARK_RET` conductor, run to the branch and left there. `L2-M 8` is held as the fused park feed for the same reason. The A3 wiper-park leg is specified **clamped and 12 V tolerant** at the resistor sub-assembly, so no replacement motor in any of the five families can damage an input. Two cavities buy the whole replacement population.
*2026-09-11 · closes 00.02*

There is no automatic climate control in this car and none is planned; the outside reading is for display, and the cluster shows it beside cabin temperature. Nothing is stranded — the feed never reached a part.

Both terms go into `retired.csv` in both projects so they cannot return by accident.

**D-339 — Two routing rules the production-car benchmark earned: everything enters a module from below or with a drip loop, and the shielded tach core never runs beside a coil lead.** Agent, 2026-09-12, carrying out `G7` and `G11`.

**Water (`G7`).** The classic Mercedes rear-SAM failure is water down a lamp seal or a blocked drain into a module. The FB's equivalents are the cowl seam and the windscreen, and the dash node sits in the footwell under both. `rules water-ingress`: every conductor enters the PMU, the dash node and each sill or rear panel **from below or with a drip loop**; nothing mounts in the **lowest 50 mm** of the footwell; the PMU's 39-way faces **down or sideways, never up**. Written now because moving a bracket while the dash is out costs nothing and moving it afterwards costs the dash. Where the water actually goes when the drains block is `CK04`, a look at M-1 — the rule does not wait on it.

**EMC (`G11`), with one correction to the premise.** The row said "the engine leg carries the CAN2 drop and the tach line past the coils and igniters." **The engine leg no longer carries CAN2 at all.** D-318 released `L1-S1 9` and `10` to sealing plugs and moved every computer, including a future ECU, to the dash node. So the engine-bay exposure is the **shielded tach core** alone — and it is the worst run in the car, because it takes a trailing-coil negative primary past four coil and igniter leads. `rules emc-routing`: it crosses ignition leads at **90°** and never runs parallel to one within **50 mm**, with the drain to the GND bus at the dash-node end only, which the record already specified. CAN2's only remaining exposure is inside the dash, where the same 50 mm applies past the blower and wiper motor leads and the O1 pop-up motor bus.

**In the data.** `rules water-ingress`, `rules emc-routing`, `checks` CK04. Both are install rules, so they govern how L1 and the dash node are **laid**, not only how they are drawn. No wire, no part, no cavity.

**D-350 — The control panel is the DCU's faceplate, so `DP-KEY` and `L3-WIN` are deleted, `DP-DCU` gets a constant feed and a wake line, and parked operation becomes a PMU gate rather than a connector.** Camden's call, 2026-09-13, answering `00.13` — and not with any of the three options it offered. Closes `00.13`. The luxury side is `D-355`, which supersedes `D-210`.

In his words: *"Neither (a), (b) nor (c) — the premise changes. The panel is the DCU's faceplate, not its own board (this resolves D-210's open half), so `DP-KEY` is deleted and the question moves to `DP-DCU`, which gets a constant feed and a wake line. Parked operation is then gated per-feature in the PMU, not at the connector."*

**Why the premise changes.** `00.13` asked whether to buy the panel a constant feed and a wake line at `DP-KEY`, and priced three answers. All three assumed the panel was a CAN node with a board. It is not. *"A dumb faceplate has no MCU and no CAN node. It does not need `DP-KEY`'s CAN2 pair, switched 12 V and ground — it needs a local cable to the DCU sitting inches behind it in the same centre stack. Sixteen to twenty conductors for a key matrix plus rotary encoders is trivial as a ribbon and impossible as a Deutsch drop, so the local cable is the only shape that works anyway."* Option (c)'s DT-6 was buying a constant feed for a board that will not exist.

**And the scope grew.** The window switch pack moves from the console to the centre panel, so `L3-WIN` goes with `DP-KEY`. The mirror control **stays hardwired at the old E-02 position** — five conductors straight to the dash post, no DCU, no CAN. *"`DP-DCU` is a DT-6 with one spare cavity and cannot carry the mirror commands, which originate at the post in the first place. Mirror adjust is the one function where software configuration buys nothing."* That closes luxury `Q-305`, and it settles the placement D-326 left open: D-326 already ruled the mirrors move on a mechanical switch with zero electronics, and said the panel's layout would have to find room for it. It does not — the control stays where Mazda put it.

**Parked behaviour is a gate, not a power decision.** Every panel key carries an `A16` precondition **except** hatch release and fuel-door release, the two that exist to work parked. *"A16 is a ladder read, never a CAN term, so the PMU refuses regardless of what the panel sends"* — a hard floor under FT16's fail-to-off pattern, and what stops a bag bumping the defog key while the car is being unloaded. Most of it is already covered: `O15` is ON in RUN, so seat heat, the HVAC servos and mirror heat cannot be woken by a stray press. Only defog (`O4`) and the windows (`O1`) sit outside that bus.

**No retained-accessory timer for the windows.** *"A timer would instead hold the module awake after EVERY key-off, against D-248's 30 s sleep and LD17's 30 mA target, to serve a case that almost never happens."* A press reaches the DCU on its constant feed, the DCU's wake line pulls the PMU up, the window runs. The cost is a perceptible delay on the first press after sleep and nothing after that. Accepted.

**In the data.** `cavities` and `housings`: `DP-KEY` 1–4 and `L3-WIN` 1–6 deleted with both housings; `L3-S2 3–6` re-terminate at the centre panel; `DP-DCU 1` becomes a **constant** feed and `DP-DCU 6`, the housing's last spare, becomes the DCU's wake request. `fuses`: **F22**, 3 A, sealed inline off the busbar — assigned here rather than in the answer because that was the free-position job the ruling left to the record. Block A's F13 was not taken: D-274 has it for `L3-MOD`. `pins`: pin 7's wake strip gains a seventh diode-OR input, CAN2H/L drop the `DP-KEY` destination, and O10's consumer list drops the `DP-KEY` tap. `logic` `DEFOG` gains its trigger — the row read "no trigger this build", so this is the trigger and not an edit. `parts`: P124 and P129 4 → 3, P036 3 → 2, P099 4 → 3, P128 3 → 2, P035 2 → 1. `devices`: **DV52** the hardwired mirror control at E-02, **DV53** the faceplate on its ribbon, tapping `L3-S1 8` so it dims with the dash. `retired`: both housing names, in both areas.

**Two consequences worth naming.** The constant feed is a permanent draw on the always-hot busbar that did not exist before — the DCU asleep is on D-280's sleeping budget now, and `CK02` is where that shows up. And D-341's tap audit listed `DP-KEY 3` among the five 16 AWG conductors on a 13 A channel; it is four now. That body is frozen (R4) and the finding is unchanged: every one of them is a tap carrying milliamps.

**What this does not settle.** The windows share `O1` with the pop-up bus, whose retry class is `guarded` because a trip there means an obstruction — and a window reaching its stop is a legitimate spike that reads the same way. Camden: *"Needs its own ruling."* It is **`00.18`**.

**D-360 — The mirrors share one clutch line: four DCU lines on `L3-S3 5–8`, the clutch spliced at the post onto both mirrors.** Camden's call, 2026-09-21, answering `00.19`: **"a"**. Closes `00.19`.

**The problem it settles.** Luxury D-359 has the DCU drive the car's own FB mirrors, each one motor plus a clutch coil. `L4-S2 1–5` already carry five mirror lines from the dash post to the doors, but only four free conductors run from the DCU in the centre stack to the post: `L3-S3 5–8`. `DP-DCU` has no spare.

**The ruling.** Both clutch coils switch together on one line, so four lines are enough. Only the mirror whose motor is driven actually moves, so in use it behaves the same as separate clutch lines. The only thing given up is moving the two mirrors on different axes at the same time. Not taken: (b) a new 6-way `L3-S4` housing, about $10 and one more connector; (c) upsizing `L3-S3` to a 12-way, which would change the part number under the kick-down and radar pass-through lines.

| `L3-S3` | Line | DCU driver | At the post |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 | Motor common (both mirrors) | half-bridge | linked to `L4-S2 1` |
| 6 | LEFT motor | half-bridge | linked to `L4-S2 2` |
| 7 | RIGHT motor | half-bridge | linked to `L4-S2 4` |
| 8 | Clutch coils (both mirrors) | low-side | spliced to `L4-S2 3` and `L4-S2 5` |

**The assumption it rests on.** Sharing the clutch line assumes each clutch coil returns to ground, not through a motor pin. Nobody has measured it (R11). `W-332` measures it, and says so: if the coil returns through a motor pin, this ruling is contradicted and becomes a block **before anything is crimped** — (b) was the stated fallback. Nothing is bought or built until the design is complete (D-323), so the fallback costs a row edit, not rework.

**D-377 — The ICU carrier's Teensy 4.1 pin map.** CAN1 is on 22 / 23. The tach and road speed are on FreqMeasureMulti pins 2 and 3. The BT817 runs on single-lane SPI0 (10–13, PDN 9), not QSPI. Every channel's pin is now in `icu_channels.teensy_pin`. This is the agent's call (§3 small): it moves copper on a board that has not been laid out and changes no harness wire, part or price. It is step A2 of the layout guide, done before any measurement because nothing about it is measured.

**Sources.** CAN pins come from the ACAN_T4 manual (tables 2 and 5: FlexCAN1 Rx 23 / Tx 22, FlexCAN2 1 / 0, FlexCAN3 30 / 31). Analog, SPI0 and Wire pins come from the Teensy core's `pins_arduino.h` (A0–A13 = 14–27, A14–A17 = 38–41, SPI 10 / 11 / 12 / 13, SDA 18 / SCL 19). Serial2 comes from `HardwareSerial2.cpp` (RX 7 / TX 8). Capture-capable pins come from FreqMeasureMulti's IMXRT table (0–9, 22–25, 28, 29, 33, 36, 37, 42–54 on the 4.1) and FreqMeasure's page (Teensy 4.x: pin 22 only). All were read 2026-09-22. PJRC's printed pinout card was not readable as text: check it against this map when the socket footprint is placed, per A2's own instruction.

**What it settled.**
- **Tach capture vs CAN.** The record said "input capture" for IC04 / IC08 and "CAN1" for IC16. The obvious library, FreqMeasure, has exactly one Teensy 4.x pin, 22, which is CAN1's TX. So the tach and road speed use FreqMeasureMulti, on 2 and 3. The firmware has no tach capture yet, so nothing changes in code; the bench rig `tach_simulator` keeps its own 3 → 4 jumper.
- **The display bus (guide A0 #5).** `icu_channels` IC21 said "SPI1 / QSPI"; `bt817.h` drives SPI0 (CS 10, PDN 9) at 20 MHz single-lane and says QSPI is a later optimisation. The Teensy 4.1's only QSPI port is FlexSPI2 on the bottom pads, and the PSRAM (P108) is soldered there. So single-lane SPI0 it is: the firmware was right and the row changes. IO2 / IO3 are still wired, to 26 / 27, and held as inputs so a later software QSPI is not foreclosed.
- **Consequence, arithmetic.** A full-screen push is 614,400 B × 8 bit / 30 MHz ≈ 165 ms (≈ 250 ms at the 20 MHz bring-up clock). The archived "~100 ms" assumed QSPI. It is still only a page transition (D-168: dirty tiles in the loop), so nothing else moves. `params.full_push_ms` now derives it.
- **Lines the sheet has and the record didn't.** The schematic's J5 carries CAN_STB, BT817_INT, BL_EN and PG_5V, which the rows never listed. They are placed on IC16 (STB 32), IC21 (INT 24), IC13 (BL_EN 36) and IC12 (PG_5V 37).

**The map.** ADC: IC01 14 · IC02 15 · IC03 16 · IC05 17 · IC07 20 · IC14 21. Capture: IC04 2 · IC08 3. Digital: IC06 28 · IC09 29 · IC10 30 · IC11 31 · IC22 25. CAN1: 22 / 23, STB 32. BT817: 10–13, PD 9, INT 24, IO2 26, IO3 27. I²C: 18 / 19, IMU INT 33. Radio: Serial2 7 / 8, EN 34, BOOT 35. BL_EN 36, PG_5V 37. **Spare:** 0 / 1 (CAN2 / Serial1), 4 / 5 / 6 (capture), 38–41 (analog). Nothing on 42–54 (the SD slot and the PSRAM pads).

**In the data.** `icu_channels` `teensy_pin` on all 19 rows that reach the Teensy; IC21 `carrier_stage`, `on_the_wire` and `note` (SPI, and its stale "the pages are the luxury package's", D-374). `params` `full_push_ms`. The sheet's `J5` still carries ordinal numbers, and its nets are still named `QSPI_*`. Renumbering them against the socket footprint is guide step A2.4, in KiCad.

**D-378 — The PMU's frames 0x100–0x130 are a CANbus Export we define, not a layout ECUMaster fixes. Fail-open (D-251) is built from each CAN input's own default and on-timeout value.** The agent's reading of the PMU manual in the tree (S-028, `01-REFERENCE/PMU_info/PMU_Manual.pdf`, ECUMaster PMU-16/16DL/16AS/24DL User Manual v101.2.1, 2026-04-23), closing work row V-065.

**What the record believed.** V-065 and `can_messages` 0x100 said the PMU's CAN layout is "fixed by ECUMaster", so every PMU-sourced field in the ICU was "written against a guess".

**What the manual says.** The PMU has two separate transmit mechanisms:
- **The Standard CAN Stream is fixed** (p.95: "Parameters themselves are predefined (they are fixed and cannot be configured)"). It uses Base ID +0…+11, 0x668 by default on PMU-24 #1, at 20 or 62.5 Hz: status, currents, voltages and temperatures. It is not what 0x100–0x130 describe.
- **The CANbus Export is ours** (p.90: "CANbus Export allows sending any available channel of the device. Frames with any CAN ID can be transmitted on one of two CAN buses"). It allows DLC 0–8, 1–100 Hz or on an edge, and at most 500 frames/s per bus (p.91). Our four frames are 40 frames/s. CAN2 defaults to 500 kbps. The only reserved IDs are 0x012–0x017 on CAN1 (p.94).

**The limits that bind our layouts.** An Export field is 8-bit (unsigned or signed) or 16-bit (big- or little-endian), times an integer multiplier 1–1000, or raw (p.92). The manual shows no bit-packing, no multiplexing and no rolling counter on transmit. So:
- the bitfield bytes (0x100 bytes 1 and 2, 0x120 bytes 2–4) need PMU math channels that build the packed value;
- **0x130's multiplexed channel index and the byte-7 counters on 0x100–0x130 are unproven.** They are proved in the PMU client at F-009, or 0x130 becomes fixed frames instead.

**Fail-open.** Each CAN input has a default "used from starting the device until receiving the first frame" (p.89). The timeout is set per message object, in seconds. What happens on timeout is set per input: "Use previous value" or "Set value". D-251's fail-open is therefore: a safe default on every input near a control rule, with "Set value" to that same safe value on timeout. The 0x218 fault log comes from the same timeout. Whether the message-object timeout accepts fractions of a second (our 250 / 500 ms) is new check **CK13**.

**In the data.** `work` V-065 done; F-009 re-scoped (prove the Export in the client, or simplify the frames). `can_messages` 0x100–0x130 notes. `checks` CK13 (new).
*2026-09-22*

**D-379 — The DCU carrier's parts check (V-083).** The seat loads use protected low-side switches (Infineon BTS3011TE) instead of bare FETs. The window commands and mirror heat use 65 V-rated PROFET+ high-side switches (BTT6200-4ESA, BTT6050-1ERA). The mirrors run from one quad half-bridge (TI DRV8962-Q1). The servo rail gets its own 5 A buck (TI TPS54560B-Q1) and the firmware moves one servo at a time. The agent's call, closing work row V-083 as D-273 did for the ICU: every part was checked against its datasheet, and every price and suffix stays `confirm` until it is ordered.

**What the check changed, and why.**
- **The AOD4184 cannot be driven from the Teensy.** Its gate threshold is up to 2.6 V, and its on-resistance is only specified at 4.5 V and above. At 3.3 V a worst-case part is barely on, and it is not AEC-Q101. The **BTS3011TE** (TO252-5) takes a 3.0–5.5 V logic supply, is 11 mΩ (22 mΩ hot), is rated 10 A nominal, and has its own short-circuit and over-temperature protection. That protection matters on a seat heater, which is a safety load (§3). Its load-dump rating is 40 V with a 2.2 Ω load: `confirm` it against the comfort supply's clamp.
- **The high-side switches are the 24 V PROFET+ family, because of the clamp.** The SMBJ33A clamps load dump at ~53 V, and the 12 V PROFET+2 (BTS70xx) is only rated to 35 V, so it was rejected. **BTT6200-4ESA** (quad, 1 A per channel with all four on, 3.3 V inputs, VS(LD) 65 V) takes the four window commands (SN22). **BTT6050-1ERA** (4.5 A nominal, 65 V) takes mirror heat (SN16), which V-101 puts at ~3 A for the pair.
- **The mirrors use one chip.** The **DRV8962-Q1** has four independent 5 A half-bridges, 4.5–60 V, and 1.5 V logic threshold. Three drive the motor common and the left and right motors; the fourth holds its low FET on as the clutch-coil sink (D-360). The TLE94104EP was rejected as a 40 V-class part under the clamp. The mirror stall current is still W-332's; it is assumed under 1.5 A, far inside 5 A.
- **K3/K4 selects:** Nexperia **PMV37ENEA** (SOT-23, 60 V, AEC-Q101, Vgs(th) 2.3 V max). That leaves ~1 V of overdrive at 3.3 V into a ~150 mA relay coil. The on-resistance at 2.5 V is a curve, not a guarantee: `confirm` on the bench.
- **The servo rail outgrew the LMR36015.** Three servos stalled together is up to 7.5 A. A 5 A **TPS54560B-Q1** (HSOP-8, 60 V, load-dump tolerant, with a 60 V 5 A Schottky catch diode, `confirm` part), plus firmware that moves one servo at a time, keeps the realistic peak near 2.5–3 A. That rule goes to F-017. The logic rail stays an **LMR36015-Q1**, as on the ICU.
- **Current sense:** **INA180A1** (gain 20, powered from 3V3) across **two 10 mΩ 2512 ≥ 2 W resistors in parallel** (5 mΩ). These are easy to buy and share the heat. 18 A worst case (V-101) is 1.8 V at the ADC, with full scale about 33 A.
- **CAN:** **TCAN1042HVDRQ1**. The V suffix gives the VIO pin (3.3 V logic); the H suffix gives ±70 V bus-fault protection.

**In the data.** `parts` P146 (the two bucks, now different parts), P149 (the comfort stage's parts), P145 (the exact suffix). `dcu_channels` SN13, SN16, SN17, SN22, SN23, SN27 carrier_stage. `work` V-083 done; F-017 note (servo sequencing).

**D-380 — The control panel's electronics.** Nine keys on a 3 × 3 matrix with a diode on every key, four detented quadrature encoders, and the mirror thumbstick. All of it reaches the DCU on one 20-way 2.54 mm IDC ribbon, whose pinout is the new table `panel_ribbon`. The agent's call, closing work row H-007's electrical half: every part of it can be undone by editing rows, and nothing is bought, cut or wired yet. The panel's look is not part of it: where the keys and knobs sit and what they look like is the luxury package's (luxury LP20, FT14), a block when the faceplate is drawn.

**The design.**
- **Keys** (FT14's nine): ROW1 defog · hatch release · fuel-door release. ROW2 HVAC mode · recirculate · window DRV up. ROW3 window DRV down · PASS up · PASS down. One 1N4148W per key, so any combination reads true: two windows moving at once is the normal case, and a diode-less matrix ghosts on three keys. Rows are driven low one at a time; columns are pulled up and carry pin-change interrupts. **Asleep, all three rows are held low, so any key press interrupts and wakes the DCU**, which then pulls the PMU's wake strip on DP-DCU 6 (D-355, SN21). That is how the panel works with the key out.
- **Encoders:** fan, temperature, and one knob per seat. A seat knob turns clockwise from OFF for heat 1–3 and anticlockwise for cool 1–3, so heat and cool can never both be on (D-073). The interlock lives in the knob as well as the firmware. Detents and range are firmware (D-355), and there is nothing to calibrate on the panel.
- **Thumbstick** (D-359): two pots fed from the Teensy's 3.3 V on their own analog ground (ribbon pin 20), plus a push to GND.
- **The ribbon:** 20 conductors, as DV53 foresaw ("sixteen to twenty"). It carries no 12 V: the panel's illumination stays a separate lead from L3-S1 8.

**In the data.** `panel_ribbon` (new table, 20 rows); `dcu_channels` SN18, SN19, SN20; `parts` P155, P157; `devices` DV53; `work` H-007 done. F-017 does the scan, the encoders and sending 0x400 (F-016).

**D-382 — The DCU's comfort circuits: 7.5 A fuses per seat heater, 5 A per seat cooler and 5 A for mirror heat, and an 8-way comfort connector on the DCU that carries its own two ground pins.** Camden's call, 2026-09-23, answering `00.28`: **"a"**. Closes `00.28`.

Each fuse is about 1.5 times its load: **7.5 A per seat heater, 5 A per seat cooler, 5 A for mirror heat** (F14). The DCU's comfort connector (P153) is a **Deutsch DT13-08PA**, pinned as follows:
- 1–4: the four seat returns (heat driver, heat passenger, cool driver, cool passenger);

The seat return current goes to ground through the DCU board. At worst it is about 15 A, and the logic ground (`DP-DCU 3`, one size-16 contact) is rated about 13 A, so this return gets its own path. **What it forecloses, as the block said.** Peltier seat cooling. A thermoelectric unit draws about 10 A per seat, which is over these fuses and this connector. Choosing one later reopens this ruling.

Their length is a hand figure until the route is measured (R11). They are part of the luxury comfort-return harness (luxury LP49), which is the mating plug side; this build owns the receptacle on the DCU and the landing on the dash ground bus.

**D-385 — Every harness leg gets two generated drawings: a pin ladder (A) and a route map (B), in `00-electrical/diagrams/<leg>/`, rebuilt by `rx7.py diagrams`. The four sampled options are kept for a later switch.** Camden's call, 2026-09-23, in conversation after he was shown four options sampled on real L1 data.

**His words.** First: "i want a map of each leg of the harness on an easy to read diagram for my use while building and for the car record for later … we need a way to have the diagrams dialed in color coded and perfect no overlaping text or wires other the a one over one cross." Then, choosing: "all options this round are good store them for futre refrence in case i want to switch, for now follow the A and B plan for each leg, in 00-electrical make a dir diarams with a readme with these options, and a folder for each led with two files for each leg (a and b)."

**The ruling.**
- **A · Pin ladder.** One block per housing and one row per cavity, with each wire a straight line from its cavity to `cavities.lands_on`. Crossings are impossible by construction.
- **B · Route map.** The leg as it runs in the car, drawn like a transit map: each wire is its own line, stacked in branch order, so it peels off the outside of the bundle. Bends are 45° only and nothing crosses.
- **Files.** Each leg's two sheets are `A-pin-ladder.svg` and `B-route-map.svg` in `L1-engine/`, `L2-front/`, `L3-dash/` and `L4-rear/`.
- **Options kept.** The C (ELK) and D (D2) samples, and the A and B samples, are kept in `diagrams/options/` with the code that drew them. `diagrams/README.md` records each option's verdict.

**Why it is safe to generate.** This amends CLAUDE.md §1, which allowed only `DECISIONS.md` and `TODO.md`, under the same four conditions:
- the sheets are a pure projection of the record
- they are read-only
- they are rebuilt whole by one command
- nothing gates a commit on them, and `check` never looks at them

**The overlap rule, which is what makes it work.** Every label is measured with the real font before it is placed. A sheet with two touching labels, or a label on a wire, is refused and not written, and the command exits 2. The WireViz sheets (D-275 / D-276) failed because nothing checked the layout.

**Consequences in the data.** Two columns were added, both small (§3: a fact that had no column):

**D-251 — Wire is control, CAN is telemetry. Anything the PMU acts on for the engine or for safety sits on a hardwired PMU input; anything it only logs or displays may arrive on CAN2; and a CAN value ever admitted to a control expression fails open on timeout.** Camden's call, 2026-09-07, the electrical half of `Q-116`. Bus priority (a lower identifier wins arbitration) solves latency under contention — at CAN2's ~1.5 % load the worst case is one lost arbitration, about a quarter of a millisecond — and solves nothing about *source failure*: a rebooting, hung or unplugged ICU simply stops sending, and the PMU cannot tell "no message" from "no pressure". A gate that cuts on timeout kills the pump when a module hiccups; a gate that ignores timeout is silently absent whenever the module is down. Neither is an interlock. So the oil-pressure gate lives on A7 (D-249); the rpm term D-183 waits for arrives as a *secondary* condition whose timeout reads as running; and the PMU logs the ICU's rpm, oil pressure, water temperature and fuel level as received channels for display and cross-check only. *Consequence for the harness:* **fuel level becomes the ICU's signal.** `DP-ICU-B 3` taps the fuel node (`N64`), the ICU publishes it on CAN2 (luxury D-306: frame `0x218`, 2 Hz), and the PMU records it as a received channel. Three readers on the oil node (`N47` — the factory gauge, the PMU's A7, the ICU) is deliberate: a cross-check, not a duplicate, and a disagreement is a sender or wiring fault nothing else would show.

**D-279 — Protection is configured as two decisions, not one, and the policy differs by fault type.** From the 2026-09-08 benchmark against MoTeC, TI and Infineon practice; applied to `rules` and the templates on 2026-09-08 under a spent number and written here on the 2026-09-08f repair. Four refinements to D-164 / D-165 / D-175, all configuration — no wire and no part:

*Sizing.* The flat current threshold comes from the load (**~1.15× measured steady state**); the **time / I²t curve comes from the conductor**. MoTeC states that setting a limit near the device's own draw *"is unlikely to be effective"* at protecting the device — the limit exists to protect the wire. D-232 already ties gauge to limit; this ties the curve to the gauge.

*Inrush rides on the time dimension, never on the flat threshold.* Raising the threshold to stop nuisance trips buys a hole in the protection. For motors prefer a **stall timer** over a current trip — a wiper or a pop-up at stall is a thermal event, not a short.

*The motor factor goes from 1.10 to 1.25 on measured stall.* 1.10 is tighter than TI's 1.15 on *nominal*, applied to a stall figure that rises with age and with falling voltage. The consequence config cannot fix: **O1 is already at the 25 A channel ceiling against a measured 26 A both-sides stall** (LD08), so the pop-up bus has no headroom and leans on the D-186 obstruction timeout instead. O8 / O9 are held at 13.0 A by the DT contact rating (D-223), so this factor changes no existing number — it governs every figure measured from here on.

*Retry and latch are split by fault type* (`rules` retry): a hard overcurrent gets bounded fast retries, then a latch, then a flag; open-load and thermal never latch; and **no safety channel latches silently** — a latched stop lamp or headlamp must annunciate, because a latched-off headlamp at night is worse than a flickering one.

*Bulb-out annunciation on O2, O3 and O7.* Per-channel undercurrent against an expected window says a stop or headlight bulb is dead. On ECUMaster undercurrent raises a fault flag and **does not disable the output**, which is exactly right — it is an annunciator, not protection, and no logic may be built on it. This is the affordable answer to both brake lamps sharing O7, since there is no spare 15 A channel to segment into (§0 G1 carries the rows).

**D-280 — The sleeping current is a budget and an acceptance test, not an assumption.** From the 2026-09-08 benchmark; applied to `loads` LD17 and install 3.11 on 2026-09-08 under a spent number and written here on the 2026-09-08f repair. LD17 assumed *PMU 150 mA, nothing else*. A bench measurement of an ECUMaster PMU reports **under 20 mA**, and ECUMaster publishes no sleep-current specification at all. On the 40 Ah pack that is the difference between roughly **11 days and 80 days** of parking before the BMS cuts off — and a LiFePO4 gives no slow-crank warning: it is fine, and then it is completely dead, sometimes needing a charger to wake the BMS.

**Measure total sleeping current at the dash node before the dash closes** (install 3.11). Target **≤ 30 mA**, accept **≤ 50 mA** — BMW's own closed-circuit figures for the E65, which logs anything above 80 mA as a violation. Budget the wake strip explicitly: the two NPN sense stages and the bleed resistor are each a permanent path, and no published figure exists for a stage of this design.

Already correct and worth not breaking: every CAN2 drop is fed from **O10**, which de-energises in sleep. Bus traffic is what prevents standby on every PDM in the reference set, and CAN keypads are named specifically — the accessory-bus feed closed that hole before it opened.
