**D-334 — An output's healthy current is a band around a measured baseline, never a typed number; the low half of the band is the module's own Min Current parameter, and channels below the module's measurement floor get no band at all.** Agent, 2026-09-12, carrying out `G1` against the PMU manual §9.1.

`G1` asked for "a `healthy_a` band per output in `pins.csv`, recorded at shakedown, and PMU logic rows that flag a lamp channel reading under half its baseline or a motor over 1.5× it." Two things changed in the doing.

**It is one stored number, not a band, because the band is derived (R2).** `pins.baseline_a` holds the current measured live at shakedown; the thresholds are `0.5 × baseline_a` low and `1.5 × baseline_a` high, and storing them would be two more numbers to drift. Nothing about `enable_a` changes — the soft fuse protects the wire and is sized from the conductor (D-279), and health is a different question asked of the same measurement.

**The low half already exists in the module.** The PMU's **Min Current** parameter raises status **2 UNDERCURRENT** and — this is the part that makes it usable — **does not switch the output off**. D-279 already said undercurrent is an annunciator and no logic may be built on it; the manual agrees in the same words. So bulb-out costs one configuration field per channel, not a function. The high half is a written function, because the module has no "running high but under the fuse" concept.

**The floor is the real constraint, and it rules two channels out.** Below a per-class threshold the PMU clips its own measurement to zero: about **0.5 A typical and up to 2 A** on the 25 A outputs, about **0.2 A** on the 15 A outputs, about **0.1 A** on the 7 A outputs. A channel whose baseline is not comfortably above its floor cannot have a band without crying wolf every time it is on. **O21 (start relay, 0.2 A) and O22 (keep-alive, 0.2 A)** are both 7 A channels sitting on their floor: they get none, and that is written down rather than discovered at shakedown. The 25 A channels are the ones to watch — HEAD_LOW at 3.0 A and HEAD_HIGH at 3.5 A are only a little above a floor that can be as high as 2 A, which is exactly why the number is measured and not computed from `est_a`.

**In the data.** `pins.baseline_a` added, blank on every row until CK01 fills it. `rules health-band` carries the derivation and the floors. `checks` CK01 is the shakedown box: exercise each circuit, read `pmu.oN.current` in the client, record the steady figure, and treat a gap of more than about 20 % against `est_a` as a tired part rather than a bad reading — which is D-025's replacement list, arriving as a by-product.
*2026-09-12*

**D-335 — Retry is four named classes, not one rule and not three, and the pop-up bus is the one that must not retry.** Agent, 2026-09-12, carrying out `G2` under D-279's policy.

D-279 split retry and latch by fault type but left every channel carrying the same "3 retries, 5 s". `G2` asked for three classes. Writing them out produced four, because one channel does not fit any of the three and pretending it does would be worse than an extra name.

- **lamp** — 3 retries at 5 s, then latch **and annunciate**. A latched stop lamp or headlamp that says nothing is worse than a flickering one (D-279). Eleven channels, including the accessory and comfort buses and the horn.
- **motor** — 5 retries at 15 s, no latch. A wiper stalled in snow or a blower against a blocked box is a thermal event that clears; the stall timer governs, not a current spike. Wipers high and low, blower, defog.
- **critical** — 1 retry at 2 s, then off until the key leaves RUN. A fuel pump or an ignition that trips twice in three seconds is a fault, and quietly retrying it forever is how a chafe becomes a fire. Fuel pump, ignition, start relay.
- **guarded** — 1 retry, then off and flag. **O1, the pop-up motor bus, and only O1.** An overcurrent here does not mean a marginal load; it means something is physically in the way, and a hand is the something. D-279 already noted O1 has no headroom — it sits at the 25 A ceiling against a measured 26 A both-sides stall — so its real handler is the D-186 obstruction timeout and retry exists only to ride out a cold morning.
- **none** — keep-alive and the two capped swap channels.

**Why a name and not just numbers.** The point of the column is that a channel cannot quietly differ from its peers: adding an output means choosing a class, and the class is the argument. The parameters map one-to-one onto the module's own Retry count / Retry every / Retry forever fields, so this is configuration, not firmware.

**In the data.** `logic.retry_class` added and set on all 21 rows; `logic.retry` rewritten from prose to the class's parameters; `rules retry-class` holds the definitions and the reasoning. No wire, no part.
*2026-09-12*

**D-336 — The PMU cannot report an output stuck ON. The condition is inferable from output voltage against output state, it is annunciation only, and the master disconnect stays the one hard kill.** Agent, 2026-09-12, reading the PMU manual §6.1 for `G3`.

`G3`'s premise is right and it is the failure mode this whole architecture inherits: **a relay fails open, a high-side MOSFET fails short.** An output stuck on runs its load with the key out and the module asleep.

**The manual is silent, and definitively so.** The complete output-status vocabulary is `0 OFF · 1 ACTIVE · 2 UNDERCURRENT · 3 OVERCURRENT · 7 THERMAL SHUTDOWN`. Every one of them is a story about how much current is flowing through an output the module believes it is driving. There is no state for "commanded off and still live", and no fault code, LED colour or CAN bit for it.

**It is detectable, and that is worth having.** The PMU measures **voltage** on every output — 0–16 V on the 25 A and 15 A pins, 0–20 V on the 7 A pins — and exposes it as `oN.voltage` alongside `oN.active`. Battery volts with `.active = 0` is a shorted switch, and a function saying so is three comparisons. `CK07` is that check at shakedown for O2, O3, O5, O7 and O12.

**But a detector is not a stop.** The thing doing the annunciating is the module that just failed, and the output it would need to drive to warn you is on the same silicon. So the honest statement is: this buys a diagnosis, not a protection. The protection is mechanical and it is the **master disconnect** — which is why `recovery` RC01 is "open the master disconnect before you touch anything", first, before any other step, and why it says a high-side FET fails short rather than assuming the reader knows.

**One thing the row did not know.** The PMU has a built-in **inertia switch** that drops every output when measured acceleration exceeds a configurable threshold, 6 G by default. That covers the crash case properly — as long as the module is alive, which is exactly the case a shorted FET is not.

**In the data.** `checks` CK07. `recovery` RC01 and the whole dead-module branch. `rules health-band` notes that undercurrent annunciates and does not stop. The row's last question — whether **O5, the fuel pump**, gets a series relay off the key's RUN ladder as a hardware back-stop — is Camden's, as the row said, and is **`00.15`**.
*2026-09-12*

**D-352 — The fuel pump gets a series relay, K13, with its coil off the ignition switch — the one mechanical back-stop in the design against a shorted-on output.** Camden's call, 2026-09-13, answering `00.15`: **"b"**. Closes `00.15`.

**The failure this answers.** D-336 read the PMU manual and found the module has no way to report an output stuck ON: `OFF / ACTIVE / UNDERCURRENT / OVERCURRENT / THERMAL SHUTDOWN` is the whole vocabulary, and every one of them is a story about current through an output the module believes it is driving. The failure mode changed when the fuse box left the car — **a relay fails open and a high-side MOSFET fails short** — so a shorted channel runs its load with the key out and the module asleep. `CK07` detects it from `oN.voltage` against `oN.active`, but a detector is not a stop, and the thing doing the annunciating is the module that just failed.

`O5` is the one channel where that means a fuel pump running unattended rather than an inconvenience. `O21` was already covered (K9 is in series by construction), `O2`/`O3` are annoying rather than dangerous, and `O12` was rejected with option (c): ignition coils with no fuel and no cranking are a static load, and the branch around F15 and F16 is real complexity for a smaller risk.

**How it is wired, and the one thing that is not assumed.** K13 sits at the dash node. Its contact is in the `O5` conductor — the conductor is cut at the node, terminal 30 takes the PMU side and 87 the pump side. **Its coil comes from a branch off `L3-S2 1`, the ignition switch's own IG output, and deliberately not from the PMU**: a back-stop that depends on the module it is backing up is not a back-stop. With the key out the pump cannot run whatever `O5` does.

That leaves one question the drawing cannot answer: **does IG hold through START?** If it drops while cranking, K13 opens mid-crank and the pump stops at exactly the wrong moment. The factory circuit implies it holds — the coils are on IG and the engine fires while cranking — but that is an inference from a 1982 diagram about a switch in a 44-year-old car, which is precisely what R11 says not to conclude. It is **`CK10`**, five minutes with the cluster out, before the L3 leg is crimped. If IG does drop, the fix is one more conductor from the switch's ST terminal, diode-OR'd into the coil with a 1N5819 out of P071 — one wire and twenty cents, decided by a measurement instead of a guess.

**The cost, stated.** One relay's worth of new failure surface in a circuit that had none, and a fifth socket at the dash node — `K3` and `K4` are empty but earmarked for the luxury package's hatch and fuel-door release triggers (D-180, D-274), so they were never spare.

**A side effect worth having.** `recovery` RC07's limp-home fuel feed now lands on K13 terminal 87, downstream of the relay, so with a dead module the key still gates the pump exactly as it does with a live one. The dead-PMU drive got slightly safer as a by-product of this.

**In the data.** `relays` K13. `node_conductors` N69–N72. `parts` P003 4 → 5 relays, P006 10 → 11 sockets. `checks` CK10. `recovery` RC07's detail.

**D-357 — `MOTOR_BUS` takes a conditional retry class: `guarded` during a pop-up cycle, `motor` during a window command.** Camden's call, 2026-09-21, answering `00.18`: **"follow recommendations"** — option (a). Closes `00.18`.

**The problem it settles.** D-350 and D-354 put the power windows on `O1`, the pop-up motor bus, and made them work parked. D-335 had given `O1` the `guarded` retry class — one retry, then off and flag — because a trip on a pop-up means something is in the way. A window reaching its stop is a legitimate current spike every close, and reads the same way: under `guarded` a normal day's window use would latch the channel off and take the pop-ups with it.

**The ruling.** The PMU knows which consumer it just commanded, so the class follows the consumer. `MOTOR_BUS` is `popup_cycle OR window_req`, where `window_req` is any of the four window keys held in the DCU's `0x400` frame. While `popup_cycle` is true the channel is `guarded`; while only `window_req` is, it is `motor` — 5 retries at 15 s, no latch. When both are true it is `guarded`, because a pop-up obstruction is the one case that must never be retried through.

**Not taken.** (b) would spend `O13` or `O14`, the LS/CD009 swap's reserves, and re-terminate `L1-P` to `L4-P 3` — a real cost against a problem configuration solves. (c), a second PMU, is the answer only if channel pressure keeps recurring. (d), key-on-only windows, is the fallback if the conditional config proves hard to read or test; it stays available because nothing physical changes either way.

**What it costs.** One output now has two protection personalities, which is harder to read and easier to get wrong — so the rule is written into `rules` `retry-class` with MOTOR_BUS named as the only conditional channel. It does nothing about the two loads sharing the 25 A ceiling (D-279, LD08); the D-186 obstruction timeout remains the pop-ups' real handler.

**In the data.** `_schema` `logic.retry_class` widened with `conditional` (the vocabulary had no way to say it). `logic` `MOTOR_BUS`: `expression`, `retry_class=conditional`, `retry`. `rules` `retry-class`: the `conditional` class defined. Luxury `features` `FT24`: the open note replaced with this ruling. Nothing in the harness changes.

**D-363 — Window relays K5–K8 are two textbook reversing pairs: the motor leg on 30, the fused feed on 87, 87a and 85 to ground; the DCU drives 86 high-side.** Agent, 2026-09-21, a small call under §3: the record already fixed every other terminal, and a two-relay reversing circuit only works one way. Closes luxury `V-100`.

**What the record already said.** `L4-M 9–12` land each window command on **terminal 86** of K5–K8. `L4-P 3` feeds "the K5–K8 contact feed through the F8 / F9 holders". `D1 1–2` and `D2 1–2` name K5/K6 and K7/K8 as the two legs of each motor. What was blank was which contact takes which, and where 85 and 87a go. The full-folder scan of 2026-09-21 found the blank.

**The circuit.** Each door's motor sits between the 30 terminals of its pair: K5 → `D1 1`, K6 → `D1 2`, K7 → `D2 1`, K8 → `D2 2`. At rest both relays sit on 87a, which is ground, so both motor legs are grounded and the motor is braked. Energising one relay throws its leg to 87, the fused feed (F8 for the driver's door, F9 for the passenger's), and the motor runs one way. The other relay runs it the other way. Coil return 85 goes to ground at the sill (`SILL-GND`). The command arrives on 86, so the DCU **sources** 12 V into it: four high-side outputs (luxury `sensors` SN22).

**Why it's small.** Nothing is built or bought (D-323). Undoing it means editing rows. No new part is needed, and no conductor is added or moved: every wire named was already in the record, and only its terminal letter is new. It is the standard way to reverse a DC motor with two SPDT relays, and a builder would call it obvious.

**What stays `confirm`.** Which way is "up" depends on how the motor is wired inside the door. If the glass goes down on the UP key, swap `D1 1`/`D1 2` (or `D2 1`/`D2 2`) in the door harness, a row edit before it's built. Up and down on one side must never be driven together: the firmware interlocks them (luxury F-017).

**In the data.** `relays` K5–K8 `c85`, `c30`, `c87`, `c87a`; `cavities` `D1 1–2`, `D2 1–2` `src`. Luxury: `sensors` SN22 (new), `work` V-100 done.

**D-370 — The DCU picks hatch or fuel door by grounding K3's or K4's coil during the O10 release pulse.** Camden's call, 2026-09-21, answering `00.23`: **"a"**. Closes `00.23`. First he asked: *"could the be configured in a ladder like sensor situaion aka the dcu sends a different signal down the same wire and the pmu act accordingy?"* The answer, given in chat before he ruled: no. A ladder carries *information* into the PMU, and the PMU already gets that information over CAN (0x400). What's missing is something that physically steers power to one of two passive solenoids on one wire, and all eight PMU analog inputs are used anyway. He then chose (a).

**The problem.** D-354 found no free PMU output, so both release solenoids stay on O10, and ACCESSORY gains a short self-clearing release pulse. With both solenoids hanging off O10, one pulse fired both: pressing hatch also popped the fuel door. The K3/K4 sockets meant for this were empty, with nothing driving their coils.

**The ruling.**
- **Wiring.** K3 (hatch) and K4 (fuel door), ISO micro SPDT relays with an integral coil diode (luxury LP51), each take O10's release branch (N85) on terminal 30 **and** on their coil terminal 86. Their 87 goes to the solenoid (`L4-M 3` hatch, `L4-M 4` fuel door). Their coil return, 85, runs to the DCU on `DP-DCU-B 10` / `11` (N86).
- **Selecting.** The DCU grounds the chosen relay's 85 before it asks the PMU for the pulse, and holds it through the pulse. Only that relay's coil sees power and ground together, so only that solenoid fires. Outside the pulse the coils have no power at all, so a stuck DCU output cannot fire anything.

**Not taken.** (b) both opening together, and (c) a PMU output of its own (there are none free, and O13/O14 are the LS swap's).

**Still to confirm.** The solenoids' current sizes the relays and N85's gauge (16 AWG is marked `confirm`). D-180's "own fuses" for the release branches have no rating yet.

**In the data.** Electrical: `relays` K3, K4 (every terminal, type, label); `cavities` `L4-M 3/4` (source through the relays) and `DP-DCU-B 10/11` (the select lines); `node_conductors` N85, N86 (new), N24 (O10 tap); `housings` DP-DCU-B (cavities 9–11 now used, 12 spare). Luxury: `sensors` SN23 (new); `parts` LP51, LP14; `work` V-083, F-017.

**D-375 — The door and A8 wake stages are pulse (edge) stages: one 1 µF film capacitor per side, so a door left ajar or a stuck horn contact wakes the PMU once and can never hold it on.** Camden's call, 2026-09-22, answering block `00.26`: **"b"**. Closes `00.26`.

**The ruling.** Option (b) as the block put it: the same 2N3904 stages A10 worked out (an emitter-follower that switches the sense excitation on only while O22 is low, a sense NPN on a 1M / 560k divider, a follower output into wake-strip pin 7), plus one ~1 µF film capacitor per side so the stage delivers a pulse when a switch closes rather than a level for as long as it stays closed. Not taken: (a), held stages at $0, under which a door left ajar keeps pin 7 high until the BMS cuts off.

**Why.** D-248's promise that a stuck door cannot hold the car awake stays true in hardware, not only in KEEP_ALIVE's logic. The hazard still flashes with the key out: the pulse wakes the PMU and the `sleep` rule keeps it awake while A8 reads HAZARD.

**The risk carried.** The pulse must outlast the PMU's boot, and no document gives that time. CK12 item (iii) measures it on the bench before anything is soldered, and the capacitor value is sized from that reading. Until then ~1 µF is `confirm`.

**In the data.** `parts` P158 (new): 1 µF film capacitors, a pack of 5 (2 used; rounded up to a sane pack, §3), about $1. `P072` used_for says what the ten 2N3904s now do. `work` A10's gate is met; it stays open for the agent to write the stage values (§6.1). `rules` `sleep` and D-248 are unchanged: this ruling is what keeps them true.
*2026-09-22 · closes 00.26*

**D-381 — The door and A8 wake stages' values.** The agent's call, closing work row A10 on the topology A10 found and the pulse D-375 ruled. The values are the new table `wake_stages`. Nothing is bought: every part comes from P072 (2N3904), P069 (the E24 kit), P071 (1N5819 spares) and P158 (the film capacitors). Every value is `confirm` until CK12 measures the three facts no document gives.

**Per side, three 2N3904s, plus one shared:**
- **Excitation, only while asleep.** Q1, a follower off the F3 switch supply, feeds the ladder line through **220k**. Awake, the shared Q0 (driven from O22) holds both Q1 bases at 0 V, so the line sees only the PMU's own 10 kΩ pull-up and the readings don't shift. Q1's E-B junction then sits 4.1 V reverse-biased, under its 6 V limit.
- **Sense.** Q2 reads the line through a **1M / 560k** divider. At rest (the 47k baseline, D-368) the line sits at 1.99–2.41 V over 12.0–14.4 V, putting Q2's base at 0.71–0.86 V: on. With the highest-resistance pressed state (19.4k) the line is 0.92–1.11 V and the base 0.33–0.40 V: off, even hot. Awake, the line is at 4.1 V, Q2 is hard on, and **no pulse is ever made while the PMU is already awake**. The thin margin is cold at 12.0 V at rest, which CK12 reads.
- **The pulse (D-375).** Q2's collector (100k pull-up) rises on a press. A **1 µF** film capacitor carries that edge to Q3, a follower held off by **470k**, which drives the wake-strip input into the strip's 10 kΩ drain at about 10 V. That fixes the failure A10 found in the v2 stage, which reached only ~1.1 V. The pulse lasts roughly C × 420 kΩ ≈ 0.4 s; 2.2 µF would give ≈ 0.9 s. A **1N5819 clamp** on Q3's base takes the negative edge when the switch is released, which would otherwise exceed the 6 V limit. A held switch makes one pulse and nothing more, so a door left ajar cannot keep the car awake (D-248).

**What CK12 settles:** (i) the pins' resistance to ground with the PMU unpowered; (ii) pin 7's switching threshold and current; (iii) the PMU's boot time, which sizes the capacitor. Plus the cold rest margin. If a reading moves a value, the row changes before anything is soldered (E7 and E15 wait on A10).

**In the data.** `wake_stages` (new table, 27 rows). `parts` P069 and P071 used_for. `checks` CK12 note. `work` A10 done.

## Power backbone and battery

*20 live — D-061 D-062 D-063 D-064 D-145 D-198 D-203 D-229 D-234 D-235 D-238 D-239 D-241 D-246 D-316 D-319 D-321 D-337 D-347 D-351*

**D-061 / D-091 — The starter feed and the PMU feed are separate runs from the battery post; the PMU feed is 2 AWG.** Cranking pulls 300–500 A briefly and cannot pass through a Class-T sized for the module feed. The master disconnect sits in the PMU leg, so opening it isolates the electrical system while the starter cable stays passive. 2 AWG (not 4) because it is sized for the swap engine, not the 12A — about $40 more now against pulling the tunnel a second time.

**D-062 — Main protection is Class-T (Blue Sea 5007100 block, 5114 150 A fuse), mounted as close to the positive post as physically possible.** LiFePO4 delivers enormous short-circuit current and Class-T is the only common fuse with the interrupt rating to break it. The cable between post and fuse is the one length that can never be protected — keep it inches long. Not economised, ever.

**D-063 — The battery mounts on a backing plate under the floor, not through sheet metal alone.** A 15 lb mass with live terminals becomes a projectile in a crash; the plate turns a tearing load into a shear load. NOCO BG27 box (D-207), hold-down, M8 grade-8 hardware.

**D-064 — A pull string goes into the tunnel beside the 2 AWG feed.** The rear leg follows the same route later, and adding it without the string means dropping the console again.

**D-145 — First power-up of the dash node is through a 5 A fuse in the main feed, not a bench supply.** Enough for the PMU to boot and talk over CAN; anything shorted blows a $2 fuse instead of melting 2 AWG. Verify, then fit the Class-T.

**D-198 — The alternator gets its factory-spec excitation circuit: O12 → F15 (7.5 A) → L1-S1 2 → alternator BW; the charge-lamp sense WB gets its own conductor, L1-S2 8 → DP-CLU 8.** Reading factory sheet A exposed that an earlier plan had repurposed the BW feed as a sense input — the new harness would never have excited the alternator at all. This is also the prime suspect for the observed no-charge (D-179: 11.4 V at idle): the factory BW path ran through the emissions-era connectors the delete disturbed. The unit is kept and judged at commissioning on correct wiring; replaced only if it still refuses to charge.

**D-203 — The starter run is protected by an MRBF (Blue Sea 5191 holder, 5187 200 A) on the post; the alternator charges through the starter cable via F18 (100 A MIDI) at the starter stud, as the factory did through its fusible link; K9's contact feed is F17 (30 A MIDI) at the same stud.**

**D-203(g) / D-207 — Fine-strand copper welding cable for the 2 AWG runs (loomed and grommeted), closed-barrel tinned lugs hydraulically crimped; bought as fixed lengths 45 ft red / 25 ft black.** Marine-tinned cable costs about twice as much for no benefit inside loom.

**D-203(d) / D-207 — Crimpers: one IWISS solid-contact Deutsch crimper (sizes 12/16) and an open-barrel ratchet crimper for the SICMA terminals, each accepted only after three practice crimps pass the pull test (16 AWG 20 lbf · 14 AWG 34 lbf · 12 AWG 45 lbf); a hydraulic crimper for every lug.** The genuine HDT-48-00 is the gold standard; the pull test is what makes a cheaper tool acceptable.

**D-229 — No battery box.** Camden's call, 2026-09-03: the NOCO BG27 leaves the design and the Amazon cart. The backing plate, hold-down and M8 grade-8 hardware of D-063 still carry the crash case — the box was never the structure. What the box *did* provide and now has no owner is terminal insulation and debris protection for a live post in an open cargo bin, so a replacement means of covering the terminals is required before the battery is installed (`Q-103`). Supersedes the box in D-063 and D-207, and the "in a NOCO BG27 box" wording in `01-DESIGN/DESIGN.md` §2. Answers V-093.

**D-246 — 1/0 for the starter feed, and a dedicated 1/0 cranking return from the rear stud to the engine block.** Camden's call, 2026-09-04, answering `Q-106` — *go bigger and safer for both*. The feed settles an ambiguity the data carried in two rows ("1/0 (or 2 AWG)") against a cart that bought neither consistently: 18 ft of 2 AWG costs about 2 V at 400 A, and 1/0 hands half of that back on the engine that is hardest to start when it is flooded.
